You are taking over the highest-priority Bifrost work: making taint analysis incremental so a one-line edit on a 353k-line Rust repository (Vector) is re-analyzed in seconds, for a stage head-to-head against stock CodeQL. 

Read first, in this order, from /home/jonathan/Projects/bifrost3 (fetch origin; read with `git show origin/<branch>:<path>`):
2. The design principles: PR #4702, branch docs/name-resolution-chapter, docs/src/content/docs/design/name-resolution.md. The three principles that govern this work: SQLite is the primary cache read by SQL; per-file materialization keyed by blob id turns an edit into O(1); heap caches only to avoid recomputing from SQL, never as the primary store. Owner notes: query performance outranks index-time write cost, but do not materialize what is cheaper to re-derive; Rust first, built as one implementation of a generic engine.
3. The ExecPlan: branch taint-partial-flows-plan, .agents/plans/taint-per-file-partial-flows.md (commit 13668a5375). It is self-contained: purpose, context, milestones M0-M5, gates, decision log. Merge that branch into each lane's branch so the plan file travels with the work, and keep the plan's Progress / Decision Log / Surprises sections current.

Rules the owner set for how you work: you write all design (schema columns, port encoding, invariants) yourself and give children explicit specs; children inventory, measure and implement, never design. "Highest priority" means you should parallelize across children where you can usefully do so. Children run builds through normal cargo/mbx (never redirect target/ or bypass mbx), nextest --max-fail 100 with BIFROST_PARALLELISM=1 RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1 and host cache access. Commits: plain-language multiline messages. PRs: branch from origin/master without tracking, push with an explicit refspec (push.default=upstream sends new branches to master otherwise), draft PR, merge master before opening and before ready, `gh pr ready` when every gate passes, never push to a ready PR without `gh pr ready --undo`; the MergeMarshall queue lands it. 

State at handoff (2026-10-08):
- M0 is running in the previous session as two measurement lanes, I will message you when their results have landed. 
- Other lanes running in the previous session, do not touch their branches: rust-unit-summary-readers (M5 step 2 of the per-unit resolution summary, Rust readers off rust_crate_*), rust-taint-call-target-demand and #4664 (demand-driven call-target and occurrence-target resolution in RQL; these make the per-frontier resolution in M3 cheaper; merge them into your M3 lane when they land), tree-sitter-rust-0.24.5 (grammar gaps on Vector), and model PRs in bifrost-packs / bifrost-premium-packs for std/tokio write identities. Known baseline failures on master: analyzer::rust::selected_reverse::tests::scoped_reverse_uses_prepared_overlay_reference_inventory and analyzer::store::resolution_operation::rust_reverse_rows::tests::reverse_inventory_treats_unexpanded_proc_macros_conservatively.
- Vector pinned checkout: vectordotdev/vector at eaae4724689f0be9b3d163bec202571aa82f5bcb, copy at /tmp/h2h-targets/vector (copy before editing). CodeQL-faithful cleartext-logging policy and models: /home/jonathan/Projects/bifrost3/.mj/agents/f20b5a894af85903aa86ec3288aa8bd9/. The demo edit: /home/jonathan/Projects/bifrost3/.mj/agents/3f69867455b9082f16415a16e4d72369/leak-edit.patch (CodeQL reports it in 12:59 via build-mode=none; 13:05 diff-informed). Owner latency targets: under 10 s warm in a persistent session, under 1 min in a fresh process. Not sure yet if those are reasonable.

Your sequence: M1 (semantic IR rows per blob at parse time, lowerer stops reading the model overlay, read-through cache, round-trip differential, measurements) -> M2 (partial-flow rows, differential against the solver's intra-procedural propagation) -> M3 (per-query composition over rows, calls resolved only on the frontier, model contracts at call ports; gate = equality with the M0 oracle on all four captures and the Rust CodeQL parity suite, plus timings) -> M4 (diff-scoped mode, three-edit gates, incremental_equivalence cases) -> M5 only if M3 measurements justify it. Each milestone is its own PR. Report to the owner at each milestone with the gate results and the numbers, and ask the owner only for the migration number and anything that changes the Decision Log.

The M1 numbers show where the cost moved rather than disappeared: lowering every Rust blob once at index time costs 84 s of thread time on Vector (38 s of wall clock on this host), and the rows cost 25% more cache. **Three M3 decisions for you**, recorded in the plan as owner questions:

1. **Engine selection rule.** During the rollout, a taint policy whose bound endpoints all sit in Rust blobs with complete IR and partial-flow publications, and that uses no store ends or entry points, runs on the composition engine; everything else stays on the ICFG engine. The rule is evaluated once per compile from the inputs, written to the run's execution record, and pinned by a test. It is not a fallback on failure. The design chapter forbids two resolvers with a hidden fallback; this is two engines by explicit rule, retired when every language publishes partial flows. Confirm or redirect.
2. **Gate for diagnostics.** A sink-first frontier visits a different procedure set than source-rooted regions, so run-incomplete diagnostics will not match the oracle one for one. Proposed gate: findings equal on every capture (sink location, labels, origins, witness step locations), completion type equal, distinct diagnostic codes a subset of the oracle's, parity and incremental-equivalence suites unchanged; diagnostic counts recorded, not gated.
3. **Stores and entry points** stay on the ICFG engine in M3.

M3-a landed with its gates green and found two real design gaps, both of which I'm resolving now:

- **Heap input ports.** M2 seeds only parameters, receivers and call results, so a callee that reads a field of a parameter the caller tainted has no port to receive that taint, and M3-a had to approximate the other direction by dispatching every call in a visited procedure. The fix is in M2: a `Heap` port rooted at a parameter or receiver is also an input port, seeded at entry, whenever a relation reads from it. Then the backward search answers it through callers like any other entry port, demand-driven.
- **Call context.** The lane correctly matched returns to the call they came from and let a demand climb to callers only when it originated in that procedure (or at a capture root). That is the intended semantics; the spec text was too loose and is corrected.
